lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- The Meeting With the Americans
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Monaco | Lesson 5 -- The Meeting With the Americans

listenings.text: I have run calls with people from a dozen countries, and the thing I wish somebody had told my colleagues abroad is this: on an American call, silence is not read as politeness. It is read as agreement, or as absence. Nobody is going to stop and ask what you think, not because they do not care, but because the meeting has forty minutes and eleven items. If you wait for a gap, there is no gap. What actually works is small and slightly uncomfortable. Say the person's name. Say sorry, can I jump in. Say I want to make sure we are on the same page. Those five words are not impolite here, they are the signal that you want the floor, and once you have said them once, people leave you room the second time. The colleagues who go quiet on my calls are almost never the ones with the weakest English. They are the ones being polite in a way that costs them the meeting.

The most useful habit I ever picked up costs ninety seconds and I stole it from a colleague in Dublin. At the end of every call, before anybody leaves, somebody says out loud what was decided, who is doing it, and by when. That is it. It sounds obvious and almost nobody does it, and the reason it matters is that half the room heard a different meeting. Somebody heard a decision where there was a discussion. Somebody heard a maybe where there was a no. If you are the person who says it out loud, two things happen. The room corrects you immediately, which is exactly what you want, and you become the person whose version of the meeting is the one in writing. That is a surprising amount of quiet influence for something that takes less time than saying goodbye.

extra_audio.text: Somebody says at the start that they have a hard stop, so the decisions come first. A point is raised that affects only two people, and it is taken offline. Somebody pushes back on a deadline instead of agreeing to it in silence. The finance team is looped in on the item nobody in the room can answer. And before anybody leaves, one person says out loud what was decided, by whom and by when.
